clue.text: Around Northern fair, masterpiece turned up, depicting flower

definitions.note: crossword sense: a flower is something that flows, i.e. a river

indicators.note: in a down entry, turned up means the whole assembly is read from the bottom upwards
around tells us the masterpiece word encloses the other pieces

parts.note: a gem is a prized piece of work
OK means middling, all right, as fair does

explanation.surface: An art critic describes a northern fair where a masterpiece shows a painted bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' and 'turned up' give GNOKEM read upwards in this down entry. 'Flower' wants to be a bloom in the painting; it is something that flows.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mekong is a great river of South-East Asia, and a river is a thing that flows.

clue.text: Perhaps 1 in 5 fail to put in donation

indicators.note: the word for fail is put in, i.e. inserted into the donation word

parts.note: a grant is a sum given
to die is to fail or stop working, as an engine dies

explanation.surface: A charity reports that one donor in five fails to give anything.
explanation.walkthrough: '1 in 5' looks like a statistic about donors; it is a slope, rising one unit for every five across.
explanation.definitionFit: A slope expressed as a ratio, such as one in five, is an example of a steepness measure.

clue.text: Really briefly, this person let me see paintings by him?

definitions.note: the question invites naming the artist whose works these would be

indicators.note: briefly means the word is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: very means really, as in very good
the setter speaking of themselves: me
er is the hesitation sound a speaker makes while thinking, as let me see does

explanation.surface: Someone asks, rather briskly, whether they might view the pictures by a certain artist.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: the answer is the painter himself, the 'him' whose paintings the speaker wants to see.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dutch master of Girl with a Pearl Earring is the artist whose works would be called paintings by him.

clue.text: Gravy boat's side is upright

parts.note: jus is a thin gravy or meat juice, from French

indicators.note: side here means the edge letter of the word, its final one

explanation.surface: A kitchen remark that the side of the gravy boat stands vertical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upright' is moral, not vertical: honest and fair.
explanation.definitionFit: An upright person is fair and honourable, a synonym of the adjective for someone who deals rightly.

clue.text: Extremist's from Danish region, and going to rising

indicators.note: going means the word and departs from the region's name

parts.note: Zealand is the Danish island and region containing Copenhagen

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means the word to is read upwards

explanation.surface: An extremist who comes from a Danish region is setting off for somewhere on the up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going' strips a word from the region, leaving ZEAL, and 'rising' gives OT in this down entry. The 's after the definition stands for 'is', a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A zealot is a fanatical, uncompromising partisan, the same sort of person as an extremist.

clue.text: Loose belt brought about blunder with one's pants

definitions.note: British slang for very bad, rubbish

indicators.note: brought about means the loosened belt letters are brought around the others
loose tells us the letters of belt are slackened into a new order

parts.note: to err is to make a mistake
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A slack belt causes an embarrassing blunder involving someone's trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loose' rearranges BELT to T...BLE, which is 'brought about' ERR and I. 'Pants' is British slang for awful, not trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang something pants is dreadful or useless, matching a word meaning very bad.

clue.text: Communication system down? One's possibly used to the drill

parts.note: feeling down is feeling blue

parts.words: One's possibly used to the drill
parts.note: a playful hint at something a dentist drills: a molar or incisor

explanation.surface: A communication system has failed, and one person is quite accustomed to the routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Used to the drill' suggests familiarity with routine; here it means subjected to the dentist's drill.
explanation.definitionFit: A short-range wireless protocol linking phones, headsets and speakers is a communication system.

clue.text: You texted message, latterly interrupting drink to finish

parts.note: in text-speak, you is written as the single letter U

indicators.note: interrupting means a letter breaks into the middle of the drink word

parts.note: to sup is to drink

indicators.note: latterly picks out the final letter of message

explanation.surface: Someone texts a message about finishing off a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhaust a supply entirely is to finish it, a phrasal verb synonym.

clue.text: Smartened appearance before office tottie finally returned

parts.note: pre is the prefix meaning before

indicators.note: finally picks out the last letter of tottie
returned means the word for office is written backwards

parts.note: a den is a study or private office

explanation.surface: Office gossip about a glamorous colleague who turned up looking smart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tottie' is British slang for attractive women. The charade runs PRE, E, then DEN reversed, despite the clue's order.
explanation.definitionFit: To preen is to groom oneself carefully, so having preened means having smartened one's looks.

clue.text: Forward, in commentary, unleashed ball at Old Trafford

indicators.note: commentary is spoken aloud, so the word is what is heard

parts.note: Old Trafford is a Test cricket ground in Manchester, where a ball is delivered by a bowler

explanation.surface: A broadcaster describes a forward unleashing a shot at Manchester United's stadium.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Trafford suggests football, where a forward plays; but it is also a Test cricket ground, where a ball is bowled.
explanation.definitionFit: A forward person is brash or presumptuous, a synonym of audacious.

clue.text: Type of road copper perhaps controlled with an Alsatian

parts.note: Alsace is in France, and un is French for an
copper is an example of a metal
led means controlled or directed

explanation.surface: A police officer controlling a road with an Alsatian dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' and 'Alsatian' paint a police dog handler; the Alsatian is a person from Alsace speaking French.
explanation.definitionFit: A road without a hard stone or tarred surface is described in Britain as lacking metalling.

clue.text: Vast garden ants regularly frequented

indicators.note: regularly means every other letter of the phrase is visited

explanation.surface: A huge garden that ants visited often.
explanation.definitionFit: Something vast is enormous, a synonym of the adjective for very large size.

clue.text: Stimulating outlet worker holding conversation at the entrance

indicators.note: holding means the exit word contains the letter

parts.note: an exit is a way out or outlet

indicators.note: at the entrance picks the opening letter of conversation

parts.note: the worker ant is the crossword's stock worker

explanation.surface: A shop worker is chatting by the doorway of an outlet store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outlet' suggests a shop, but here it is a way out.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective this word means having a stimulating, arousing effect, like a stimulant drug.

clue.text: Kid presenting female with fresh roses — one opens up

parts.note: to kid is to con or fool

indicators.note: fresh means the letters of roses are made anew

explanation.surface: A child presents a woman with a bouquet of fresh roses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kid' looks like a child but is a verb meaning to fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who admits their sins or secrets opens up; also a priest hearing such admissions.

clue.text: Risk breaking into account that's drained with gold accessory

indicators.note: breaking into means the risk word goes inside the remaining letters
drained means account is emptied of its inner letters, leaving its ends

parts.note: a bet is a risk or wager
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A gambler raids an empty bank account with the help of a golden accomplice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Accessory' looks like jewellery but is the legal sense: an accomplice to a crime.
explanation.definitionFit: In law an accessory is someone who helps commit a crime, i.e. an accomplice or helper.

clue.text: Lottery support, unspecified number, nevertheless uplifting

parts.note: a bra is a supporting undergarment
n is the algebraic symbol for an unspecified number

indicators.note: in a down entry, uplifting means the word is read upwards

parts.note: but means nevertheless or however

explanation.surface: Support for a lottery from an unknown number of people, though it is uplifting.
explanation.walkthrough: A bran tub is a British fairground lucky dip: prizes buried in bran.
explanation.definitionFit: A lucky-dip barrel of buried prizes is a game of chance, a kind of lottery.

clue.text: Ignorant Yankee's hesitating

parts.note: unread means uneducated, not having read books
Y is Yankee in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An uninformed American is dithering.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone not prepared is slow to act, so hesitating fits the sense of unprepared.

clue.text: Decorator may apply this row, coating Iain's chimney upwards

indicators.note: in a down entry, upwards means the assembled letters read from the bottom
coating means the row word wraps around the chimney word

parts.note: a row is a loud noise
Iain is a Scottish name; lum is Scots for a chimney

explanation.surface: A dispute over coating a Scotsman's chimney.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coating' gives NOISLUME, and 'upwards' reads it bottom to top. Iain's name signals a Scots word; 'Decorator' suggests a person, but the definition is what the decorator uses.
explanation.definitionFit: A water-based wall paint is what a decorator would roll onto walls and ceilings.

clue.text: False celebrity, with awful clothing

indicators.note: clothing means the awful word is wrapped round the celebrity word

parts.note: bad means awful
a star is a celebrity

explanation.surface: A fake celebrity wearing terrible clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clothing' looks like garments but is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Applied to things, this means spurious or not genuine, as in a bastard form of a word.

clue.text: Maybe saloon drivers describing the coating

parts.note: a saloon is one kind of bar in a British pub

indicators.note: describing in its sense of drawing round: the drivers' letters go around the

parts.note: the AA is the Automobile Association, the British motoring organisation

explanation.surface: Saloon car drivers describing the paintwork on their vehicles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saloon' suggests a car beside 'drivers', but it is a pub bar; 'coating' means fabric for coats, not a layer.
explanation.definitionFit: Barathea is a fine woollen fabric used for coats and uniforms, so it is a kind of coat material.

clue.text: Endless quarrel about current new weapon

indicators.note: about means the trimmed quarrel word goes round the current symbol
endless means the quarrel word loses its last letter

parts.note: to argue is to quarrel
I is the physics symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: An everlasting argument about a modern weapon of the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' cuts ARGUE to ARGU; 'about' wraps it round I, giving AIRGU, then N.
explanation.definitionFit: A gun firing pellets by compressed air is a kind of firearm or weapon.

clue.text: Supply online joke?

parts.note: E is the prefix for electronic, as in e-mail, meaning online
a quip is a witty remark

explanation.surface: Asking whether to provide a joke over the internet.
explanation.definitionFit: To supply someone with what they need is to furnish or fit them out.

clue.text: Might stores start to denounce cosmetic?

indicators.note: stores means the might word holds the letter inside it

parts.note: might means power or strength

indicators.note: start to picks the first letter of denounce

explanation.surface: Would shops begin condemning a beauty product?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Might' looks like a verb opening a question; it is the noun meaning strength. 'Stores' is not shops but holds.
explanation.definitionFit: Face powder is a classic make-up product, an example of a cosmetic.

clue.text: Properties built by Scottish island resident in rocky strait

indicators.note: resident in means the island sits inside the rearranged strait letters
rocky means unsteady, so the letters of strait are shaken up

parts.note: Bute is an island in the Firth of Clyde

explanation.surface: Estate agents describe homes built by an islander in a rocky channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rocky' rearranges the strait into ATTRIS, and 'resident in' sets the island inside it. 'Properties' are qualities, not houses.
explanation.definitionFit: Properties in the sense of characteristic qualities or traits match this plural noun exactly.

clue.text: Gathering time for root vegetable

parts.note: a bee is a social gathering, as in a sewing bee

explanation.surface: Harvest time for root crops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gathering' suggests harvesting the crop; it is a noun, a social gathering such as a spelling bee.
explanation.definitionFit: Beet, such as beetroot or sugar beet, is a plant grown for its swollen root.

clue.text: Admit being stuck on issue's centre spread

indicators.note: being stuck on means the admit word is attached after the other letter
centre picks out the middle letter of issue

parts.note: to own is to admit, as in own up

explanation.surface: Confessing to being fixated on a magazine's centrefold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue's centre spread' suggests a magazine centrefold; 'spread' is the definition, as seeds are scattered.
explanation.definitionFit: Seed that has been scattered over the ground has been spread, a past participle synonym.

clue.text: Couple, anyone can see, preferred over Australian — such as him?

definitions.note: a question pointing back to the Australian: a man typical of that country

indicators.note: preferred over means one letter is chosen in place of the Australian letter

parts.note: a brace is a pair or couple
U is the British film certificate for universal viewing, suitable for anyone

explanation.surface: A couple's film choice suitable for all is chosen ahead of an Australian one.
explanation.walkthrough: Bruce is the stereotypical Australian man's name, so 'such as him?' refers to the Australian.
explanation.definitionFit: The stock Australian bloke of comedy sketches is called Bruce, so the name is an example of one.

clue.text: Protected building again, restoring order (covering of earth)

indicators.note: covering means the rearranged letters go round the others
restoring means the letters of order are put back into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for earth, as on electrical plugs

explanation.surface: A builder protected a structure again, putting it back in order with a layer of soil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'restoring' rearranges the letters to RERO...D, which goes 'covering' the rest. 'Protected' suggests a listed building, but it means given a new top.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting a new top on a house protects it again, which is replacing the covering overhead.
